plan.chapterName: OpenStax University Physics, chapter 35: Geometric Optics and Image Formation
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a single ray diagram of image formation by a converging lens. A biconvex lens, shaded pale blue with a vertical dashed line through its center, stands upright on a horizontal optical axis. A red upward arrow to the left of the lens is the object, and its height is marked h_o by a double-headed arrow at the far left edge. Two red dots on the axis mark the focal points, each labeled F, one on either side of the lens, and a bracket from the lens center to the right-hand focal point is labeled f. Three rays leave the tip of the object. Ray 1, in red, travels parallel to the axis and bends at the lens to pass through the far focal point. Ray 2, in green, runs straight through the center without deviation. Ray 3, in purple, passes through the near focal point before emerging parallel to the axis. The three rays cross below the axis on the right, where a short red downward arrow of height h_i marks the inverted image. Horizontal brackets beneath the axis give the object distance d_o and the image distance d_i. Because each ray follows a different simple rule, their common crossing point fixes the position and size of the image by drawing alone, and the image produced here is one that could be caught on a screen.

interactions.label: Object distance (d_o)
interactions.teaches: Dragging the object changes its distance (d_o), which inversely affects the image distance (d_i) and dynamically alters the image magnification, visualizing the thin-lens equation.

Clicking a principal ray isolates its specific geometric rule—parallel to focal (1), straight through center (2), or focal to parallel (3)—showing that any two rays are sufficient to pinpoint the image.

interactions.label: Annotations
interactions.teaches: Toggling the measurement overlays maps the physical drawing onto the abstract variables (d_o, d_i, h_o, h_i, f) used in algebraic optics formulas.

demo_steps.title: Three Principal Rays
demo_steps.narration: To find where a lens forms an image, we trace three principal rays from the top of the object. Click any ray to highlight its specific path. They all converge at a single point to locate the image tip.

demo_steps.title: Defining the Variables
demo_steps.narration: Turning on the measurements reveals the geometric variables. The distances from the lens to the object (d_o) and image (d_i), along with the focal length (f), are strictly linked by the thin-lens equation.

demo_steps.title: The Lens Equation in Action
demo_steps.narration: Move the object closer to the focal point. The rays must travel further to converge, drastically increasing the image distance (d_i) and producing a larger, highly magnified image.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The geometric crossing of any two principal rays perfectly dictates the position and size of the image, physically demonstrating the algebraic tradeoffs of the thin-lens equation.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Center the horizontal optical axis in the canvas. The lens is a tall, pale blue oval. Draw the object as a solid red arrow pointing up. Ensure the three rays originate exactly from the object's tip, bend exactly at the vertical center line of the lens, and intersect precisely at the tip of the inverted image arrow. Ray 1 is red, Ray 2 is green, Ray 3 is purple. Distance brackets (d_o, d_i) sit neatly below the axis. Ensure mathematical labels (h_o, h_i, d_o, d_i, f) use an italic serif font with proper subscripts.

authoredContext:
Consider an object some distance away from a converging lens, as shown in the figure. To find the location and size of the image, we trace the paths of selected light rays originating from one point on the object, in this case, the tip of the arrow. The figure shows three rays from many rays that emanate from the tip of the arrow. These three rays can be traced by using the ray-tracing rules given above.

Several important distances appear in the figure. As for a mirror, we define do to be the object distance, or the distance of an object from the center of a lens. The image distance di is defined to be the distance of the image from the center of a lens. The height of the object and the height of the image are indicated by ho and hi, respectively. Images that appear upright relative to the object have positive heights, and those that are inverted have negative heights. By using the rules of ray tracing and making a scale drawing with paper and pencil, like that in the figure, we can accurately describe the location and size of an image. But the real benefit of ray tracing is in visualizing how images are formed in a variety of situations.

Although three rays are traced in this figure, only two are necessary to locate a point of the image. It is best to trace rays for which there are simple ray-tracing rules.

Ray tracing is used to locate the image formed by a lens. Rays originating from the same point on the object are traced—the three chosen rays each follow one of the rules for ray tracing, so that their paths are easy to determine. The image is located at the point where the rays cross. In this case, a real image—one that can be projected on a screen—is formed.

Figure shows the cross section of a bi-convex lens. Three rays originate from the top of an object and enter the lens. Ray 1 is parallel to the optical axis. Ray 2 crosses the center of the lens. Ray 3 crosses the focal point in front of the lens. All rays converge on the other side at the top of an inverted image. Ray 1 crosses the focal point behind the lens. Ray 2 is undeviated. Ray 3 becomes parallel to the optical axis. The object distance and image distances are d subscript o and d subscript I respectively. The object and image heights are h subscript o and h subscript I respectively. The focal length is f.

discrepancies: The default state hides all critical dimensions ($h_o$, $h_i$, $d_o$, $d_i$, $f$), failing to act as a drop-in replacement for the static source image until a toggle is clicked.
When enabled, the dimension lines for $d_o$ and $d_i$ are placed at the very bottom of the canvas (y=730), excessively far from the principal axis compared to the compact layout of the source figure.
Ray labels (1, 2, 3) are drawn directly overlapping the rays with opaque white background boxes, whereas the source cleanly floats them above or below the rays.
Ray arrowheads are placed at the exact midpoints of the line segments rather than at the visually distinct positions shown in the source.
evaluation.notes: The underlying ray-tracing math and interactive demo player are excellent, but the figure fails as a drop-in replacement by hiding all dimensional labels in its default state, and formats them poorly when they are revealed.

Adjust the `labelPos` coordinates for the ray labels to float them slightly off the lines, and remove their white background rectangles (`bg`).

discrepancies: The labels for the focal points ('F') are placed directly below the focal dots, causing Ray 1 and Ray 3 to strike directly through the text, rather than being safely offset to the side.
The generated image arrow on the right uses the exact same dark red color as the object arrow, whereas the source figure uses a noticeably lighter shade of red/pink to distinguish the image.
The generated lens has a flat translucent blue fill, missing the 3D-like spherical gradient shading present in the source.
The HTML UI sidebar text for 'Object distance' awkwardly wraps, splitting the variable symbol across multiple lines due to lack of a white-space constraint.
evaluation.notes: This is an outstanding, pedagogically useful interactive figure that correctly implements the thin lens equation and live ray tracing, with only minor label placement collisions and missing visual polish on the lens shading.
action_items: Offset the 'F' text labels slightly to the left and further down (e.g., x: cx ± f*S - 12, y: cy + 28) so they do not intersect the steep diagonal paths of Ray 1 and Ray 3.

Dynamically position the vertical placement of the horizontal dimension lines (dY) based on the image height (e.g., Math.max(cy + 180, imgY + 40)) so the image arrow tip doesn't collide with the dimension line when the object is moved very close to the focal point.
Change the color of the image arrow to a lighter red/pink to match the source figure's visual distinction between the object and the resulting image.
Add 'white-space: nowrap;' to the `<label>` wrapping the object distance slider in the UI panel to prevent the '(do):' text from breaking awkwardly across lines.
